title: The Complicated Society Inside Stand-Up: Even If You Tell the Joke, Will Chinese Audiences Get It?
excerpt: "The hard part of stand-up for Chinese audiences is that it asks you to appreciate values and ways of thinking completely unlike your own. You don't agree with them — but you can still appreciate them."
body:
"The hard part of stand-up for Chinese audiences is that it asks you to appreciate values and ways of thinking completely unlike your own. You don't agree with them — but you can still appreciate them."

On early-summer nights in Beijing, poplar catkins drift through the air and bright-eyed young people scatter through the hutongs in twos and threes, beer in hand. Hot Cat bar in Fangjia Hutong runs stand-up shows in Chinese and English every week; the Beijing Talk Show Club's joke laboratory there is now in its third year.

"I think Papi Jiang is a very good comedian. The reason the broadcasting regulator gave for pulling her videos was flimsy — it said her performances used coarse language, words like wocao and 'little bitch.' In modern Mandarin those barely rise above filler words. Here's something that actually happened to me. I used to have some coarse language in my act, and the relevant authorities called me in for a talking-to. Their exact words: 'Why the hell do you stand-up guys talk so goddamn dirty? Can ordinary people even fucking follow you?'"

In the dim bar, more than 70 people laughed out loud. Xijiangyue is one of the first people in China to do stand-up — a man from Gansu who has liked talking since he was a boy, and who founded the Beijing Talk Show Club, or Bei Tuo, in 2010. At the club's weekly open mic, anyone who signs up gets a few minutes on stage, which has made Bei Tuo the first place many Chinese comedians ever heard their own voice.

Six years ago, at his first public show, the room was far emptier. "I posted the event on Douban Events and five people came, two of them tourists from Shanghai who had no idea what they'd walked into," he said. "I'd even made a PowerPoint, like an investment bank, and got someone to play background music. I'd planned two hours of material and ran out in under half an hour."

Not until a show three years ago did something click. He could predict exactly where the audience would laugh, and the prediction matched the room. "I had control."

## Talk Show, Stand-Up Comedy, or a Chance to Practice English?

Stand-up comedy began in Britain and the United States in the late 19th century. Joe Wong was the first performer through whom many Chinese people learned the form existed, and he set a whole first generation of Chinese comedians going.

"Huang as in huanggua, cucumber. Xi as in xigua, watermelon," is how he often introduces himself. He went to the United States in 1994 for a doctorate in biochemistry, took the stage for the first time in 2002, and in 2010, at the Radio and Television Correspondents' Association Dinner in Washington, delivered a deadpan set in a thick Chinese accent about life as a first-generation immigrant, teasing Vice President Joe Biden along the way. The 15-minute video of that set spread widely in China.

One thing needs explaining: in China the terms tuokouxiu ("talk show") and dankou xiju ("stand-up comedy") get used interchangeably, thanks to a translation muddle. A talk show is an interview program — a host and one or several guests, usually on television: *Late Show with David Letterman*, *The Daily Show*, or, in the Chinese-speaking world, *Qiang Qiang San Ren Xing* and *The Jin Xing Show*.

Stand-up comedy reached Chinese audiences first in Guangdong and Hong Kong, brought in by the Hong Kong performer Dayo Wong, who gave it the Cantonese name dung duk siu. One comedian carries the whole show on jokes, with live back-and-forth with the room, and many performers start out in bars or comedy clubs.

The confusion is easy to explain: plenty of talk-show hosts began doing stand-up in small bars, and once they have a show of their own they will do a few minutes of jokes before the interview; comedians, in turn, are constantly invited onto talk shows. Joe Wong made his name in 2009 on *Late Show with David Letterman*.

At first there was real argument over whether Chinese audiences would take to this Western brand of humor. [In a 2010 story, *The Wall Street Journal* reported that Joe Wong's first live show in Beijing, in 2008, "was not a success" — the audience strained to catch the punchlines, and Wong remembered looking out at blank faces that were "polite but serious."](http://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703416204575146040564757682)

In the countries where stand-up was born, audiences file into dim comedy clubs and bars already smiling, and wait for the jokes over a drink. When the form first arrived in China, audiences were nervous, unsure what would happen on stage.

"Parents would bring their kids, thinking of it as family time or a lesson in Western culture, not realizing how much of the material was unsuitable. When I said it was a stand-up show in English, parents thought it was a chance to practice their English," said Tony Chou, one of the founders of the Comedy Commune club. Since 2014 the club has run ticketed shows at The Bookworm bookstore and other venues.

![Tony (courtesy of Tony Chou, photographed by Wenyinghua Studio)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702170102LnhTxBtuqWz9OQwE.jpg-w600)

Tony, 32, grew up in Jinan, Shandong. His English is fluent; after watching a video of Joe Wong he thought, "I could do that." He first trained his English stage skills at Comedy Club China, where foreign enthusiasts gathered, and today he is one of very few comedians in China who work in both Chinese and English, with English sets performed in the United States, Ireland and elsewhere.

"2013 was the year stand-up started to take hold in China. A steady audience and a circle of performers began to form," Tony said.

That year Bei Tuo got a fixed open-mic slot at Hot Cat, Joe Wong came home to build a career, and the man who did most to carry the form east appeared: the Irish comedian Des Bishop. He had come to Beijing to film a documentary about learning Chinese in a year, then founded Comedy Commune with Tony and began flying in professional comedians from abroad.

Bishop already had 20 years on stage and a successful comedy club in Ireland, and he brought Western training and organizing methods to China with a missionary's zeal.

"You could say Des Bishop taught Chinese people how to do stand-up," Tony said. "He brought a lot of Western ideas over. For instance, most people had no idea what an open mic was for. They thought it worked like kung fu — you practice alone at home, and once you've got it you go perform in a theater one day. In fact you need an audience. You need to test material."

## Who Comes to See Stand-Up?

More and more people are curious about stand-up, and willing to buy a ticket.

Comedy Commune plays rooms of 120 seats, with tickets from 80 yuan early to 120 yuan at the door. At the start it ran about one show a month and couldn't fill it; now it runs one every week or two, and nearly every show sells out. It doesn't list events on ticketing sites — the audience comes by word of mouth, and about half of any crowd is new.

![Tony (courtesy of Tony Chou, photographed by Wenyinghua Studio)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702170102kgrU3HaRMv8KmYuW.jpg-w600)

Tony can describe his core audience precisely: young professionals, in the years between graduating from college and having children. Fluent in English; international in dress and manner; mostly white-collar staff at foreign companies, employees of international organizations, and the highly educated, many of them back from studying abroad.

"Stand-up needs the performer and the audience to work on each other. The audience is part of the show, and ours is a good one," Tony said.

Young people are also the new audience Dashan — Mark Rowswell — has been working to win as he moves from traditional crosstalk to stand-up.

"Who says China doesn't do encouragement-based education? Let a foreigner manage a single 'ni hao' and a Chinese person will say, 'Your Chinese is so good! Such standard pronunciation!' Add a 'thank you' and it's, 'Wow, a real old China hand!'"

Not many people realize that Dashan, the Canadian, has not performed crosstalk in almost 20 years. The image most people still hold of him is the "international friend" in a changpao and magua robe doing crosstalk, winning the room over with faultless Mandarin delivered in something close to a CCTV anchor's cadence. Crosstalk was both his shortcut to fame in China and the ceiling on his career.

"I think crosstalk later got too traditional. In the 1980s it was mostly the new crosstalk that Ma Ji led; when I first came to it, nobody wore the changpao and magua, everyone wore ordinary clothes. After the 1990s the new style grew rarer and rarer, and audiences and performers themselves demanded more and more tradition. It went to an extreme. For me crosstalk was a foreign culture. Once I'd learned it to a certain level I wanted to improvise, and I couldn't. I didn't know how to tell my own story inside that form."

From the late 1990s Dashan left crosstalk and tried hosting, Weibo and other work he described as being a "cultural ambassador," until 2013, when Des Bishop got him to a Chinese-language stand-up show. He thought: this form could work.

But coming back to comedy through a new form meant replacing his audience wholesale.

"Young people like my stand-up; people my own age — Dashan was born in 1965 — don't. The best audiences are people born in the '80s and '90s. What I dread is a room of people born in the '60s and '70s. People my age think: Dashan, there are so many young people here tonight, you mustn't mislead them, you have to guide them properly."

For young people the name Dashan still pulls. His dated television image, a childhood memory for anyone born in the '90s, has conveniently become a supply of material for making fun of himself: ever since I took up the five-dimensional memory method, I've gone a bit senile.

In late April he played 65 minutes alone in front of 900 people at Beijing's Tianqiao Performing Arts Center. On the fame he built early on, he became the second person in China, after Joe Wong, able to headline a solo stand-up show in a large theater.

He is not the only one crossing back and forth between crosstalk and stand-up — one Chinese, one Western; one "old," one "new." Jesse Appell, a comedian from Boston, came to China as a Fulbright Scholar to research comedy, became a disciple of the well-known crosstalk performer Ding Guangquan in 2013, and also does bilingual stand-up and improv.

"A lot of people think crosstalk is old and dated. Partly it's the costumes and the teahouse setting, partly it's that crosstalk prizes studying earlier work and likes to advertise its long history. Inside the master-disciple relationship, change really is hard. I wanted to do a three-minute crosstalk piece, and my master said that would do as an opener, but the piece itself ought to be longer," Appell said.

He believes the basic technique of crosstalk and stand-up is the same, with no fundamental difference in how the comedy is written. The biggest gap between them may be how the audience sees itself. "People will watch any kind of comedy that's funny, but young audiences who want to become more Westernized want to see Western things, not traditional ones."

## An Actor Prepares, Stand-Up Edition

The American memory champion Joshua Foer says evolution has wired us to find two kinds of things especially interesting, and therefore easy to remember: jokes and sex — and jokes about sex are the easiest of all.

Because sex jokes please a crowd too easily, Bei Tuo at first forbade its members from telling dirty jokes, to build up their stamina. "Widows, breasts, backsides — mention any of them and the audience laughs," Xijiangyue said. "It's too easy."

In a form where giving offense is a key ingredient, dirty jokes are of course not off-limits. The point is to want more than a dirty joke told for its own sake.

A good joke has intelligence in it. One technique comedians lean on is remaking the logic of ordinary life, saying the most commonplace thing in a way nobody expects.

"I love going through airport security. I love it when a girl comes over and pats me down, front and then back. And then she stops. So I panicked and said I had a bomb on me. She brought over a dog: 'Go bite him.'"

Unlike some of his peers, who showed a gift for performing as children, Song Qiyu came to comedy late. He is 29, from a small town in Shanxi, and has not fully beaten his stage fright: before going on he writes his cue words on the skin between his left thumb and forefinger, and he speaks with a heavy northwestern accent and small, nervous pauses.

What came next is the inspiring part. Before 2012 he worked at a bicycle shop in Shanghai and started to doubt the point of the job — it had social value, but none for him. He went to the Chinese National Academy of Arts to study the aesthetics of comedy, a corner of drama and opera studies. In 2013 he got up at an open mic for the first time, and for three months nobody laughed once. At what he had decided would be his last set, having made peace with going back to selling bicycles, someone in the audience suddenly laughed, then shook his hand and told him he was good.

![Song Qiyu (courtesy of Beijing Comedy Center)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702170103fEPWNHtksaXn5leK.jpg-w600)

He now runs a comedy training center founded last year, holding two-day stand-up courses that teach comedy theory for 980 yuan a head. The students come from everywhere — people with depression, independent producers from the Ximalaya radio app — but few of them want to be professional comedians.

Talking to strangers is his main way of gathering material. He goes to talks and other events he finds on Douban Events, "startup pitch events, say, where all kinds of people describe bizarre things. Someone will earnestly explain how the Earth's rotation can generate electricity," he said. "You build jokes on your own suffering and other people's. If there's no suffering, go find some."

## "What It Comes Down To Is the Cleanest, Purest Freedom — I Say Whatever I Want to Say"

Many comedians will tell you that what moves them about this form of expression is that it is true.

"Don't talk in stock phrases." That was the advice Xijiangyue gave a group of stand-up students taking turns on their opening lines in a café near Andingmen. A beginner's cardinal sin: nine times out of ten the first sentence on stage is the same stiff "Hello everyone, I'm —"

Refusing stock phrases is an important step toward sounding true.

"Why does it have to be 'hello everyone'? 'Hello, all of you' works. 'Good afternoon, all of you' works. Eighty percent of Chinese people speak in stock phrases, and the moment you use one, nobody remembers you. Talk like a human being," Xijiangyue said.

Beyond showing your real self, the other thing comedians chase is a style that is unmistakably theirs — finding your voice, your character. On screen Woody Allen has been the anxious, neurotic Jewish intellectual, black-framed glasses included, consistently for decades.

Which matters more, the craft of stand-up or its spirit, is an argument the trade has been having for a long time.

In the BBC documentary *The Art of Stand-Up*, there is a conversation between the presenter and the British comedian Simon Amstell.

![A scene from the BBC documentary The Art of Stand-Up](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702170103PWaSfONb3K5UmgnF.jpg-w600)

Amstell is slight and gay, and much of his material comes from mocking his own failures; themes of loneliness and hurt put tears in his jokes. When he says something that sounds like a joke — "you're the one who should be comforting me" — he means it.

Some people do believe comedy should have a serious core. Tony says, "I think 'getting a laugh' is pandering. Good stand-up should be self-expression; it shows how you think, it shows who you are. Talking with a lot of Westerners, I find this form pure. On spectacle it can't even beat a stage play — no lights, no sound effects. What it comes down to is the cleanest, purest freedom: I say whatever I want to say."

Others hold that the laugh is the first purpose. "As long as the joke is funny it's fine, whether or not it carries a point of view. Stand-up exists to make you laugh. If the joke isn't funny, I keep my opinion to myself." That is Shi Laoban, real name Shi Jiefu, 28, baby-faced, trained in science and engineering. After studying in Britain he worked in finance for three years, then quit to become a professional comedian and comedy writer.

Disagreement isn't much of a problem in a form this individualistic. One person writes, one person performs, one person enjoys the laughter of an audience that understood or endures the silence of one that didn't. The way stand-up works is individualist to the core.

In the biopic *Man on the Moon*, Jim Carrey plays Andy Kaufman, the famous American comedian of the 1970s, who almost never told a complete joke on stage. He would stare wide-eyed and say nothing, or read all of *The Great Gatsby* aloud in a hoarse voice, or announce that he was marrying the woman who had beaten him in a boxing ring — no pattern at all, close to performance art. His strange, shifting acts drew constant argument, and yet he was accepted, whole, as a comedian.

"The hard part of stand-up for Chinese audiences is that it asks you to appreciate values and ways of thinking completely unlike your own. You don't agree with them — but you can still appreciate them," Dashan said.

## Taboos

What can be said and what can't: the standards differ sharply between the United States and China. Broadly, Chinese comedians' material rarely touches politics, while questions of political correctness have not yet drawn much attention.

One of YouTube's ten most-watched videos of 2015 was Obama on Jimmy Kimmel's show, reading out mocking tweets about himself for the "Mean Tweets" segment:

Obama's hair is looking grayer these days. Can't imagine why since he doesn't seem to be one bit worried about all that's going on.

Politics is a mainstream subject in American stand-up. Mocking politicians and the powerful is something audiences care about and join in on, and the risk is low. For reasons everyone understands, political satire of that kind is hard to find in China.

According to a person with knowledge of the matter, a stand-up show at Beijing's Fanxing Theatre Village in 2014 had the last three performances of an 18-show run canceled because it contained political satire involving the five-starred red flag. For more than a year afterward the incident also held up the group's applications to book commercial theater dates.

"In a Beijing theater you absolutely cannot talk politics. If anyone does, we kick our legs and wave our phones to get him off stage. Do it again and you're finished," the person said.

For Dashan, a foreigner's delicate position means a great deal of his material carries political weight by default. He judges the limit by whether something stays "friendly," and when a bit gets close to the line he turns it on himself. "Even when I'm satirical, I stand alongside everyone else and satirize something we all recognize together."

Few comedians in China do political material. Most say that neither they nor their audiences know or care much about politics — "Even if you let people do it now, nobody does it well."

In March, in a theater near the Bund in Shanghai, the comedian Zhou Qimo told a borderline joke built on a famous line from a political figure. Even with the word "Best Actor" laid down as setup, the more than 300 people in the room, mostly young, sat in silence, plainly missing the punchline. A little awkwardly, he said, "Looks like nobody got that."

Not getting it is probably the result of many things mixed together.

"Stand-up isn't a castle in the air. It has to sit on top of a fully developed system of public talk. A subject has to have been thoroughly discussed, there has to be a broad foundation of free speech, there has to be thick enough material already in real life, before a comedian can dig jokes out of it and reach a wide audience." That is how Shi Laoban, who doesn't much enjoy political satire, reads the present state of things.

Because stand-up can't lay out context at length the way a play or a film can, whether a joke works depends largely on how sharply the comedian can estimate what the audience already knows, the culture it carries and the talk it has been part of — find the sensitive point, and from there step "only half a step forward." That holds for politics and for political correctness alike.

Shi Laoban used homosexuality as an example of how the level a joke can reach shifts with how much a subject has been discussed.

"Chinese jokes about gay people go, 'Hey, why do you look so gay, so sissy' — that's stand-up for the mainstream cultural class of China's first-tier cities. A level up, someone points out that being homophobic is wrong. A level above that, going overboard in favoring or protecting gay people is also wrong. Americans may already be at that third stage, saying things like, 'as a white guy I'm the real minority in America now, I can't say anything anymore.' Here, you can do the second stage with urban yuppies. Nobody in China can really do the third stage yet."

By his observation, some politically incorrect habits in stand-up — sexism, slurs for neighboring countries, such as calling Koreans "sticks" — have improved somewhat in recent years.

But more subjects, politics and marginal groups among them — mental illness, pedophilia and the like — are not rare in China and still go unreported, unspread, undiscussed, so the raw material never gets the chance to become a joke.

"Do stand-up long enough and you know exactly where the line in society's public talk runs, how far an audience can go with you. Some of the jokes in my head I figure I'll be able to tell in ten years, once people's thinking has caught up," Shi Laoban said.

## Not an Industry Yet, Only a Cultural Phenomenon

"Right now the whole country has maybe 20-odd full-time stand-up comedians. Count the part-timers and it might be 50 to 60 — and that's counting only the useful ones," Xijiangyue said.

Comedy clubs are the mark of how alive a city's stand-up scene is. According to Feng Liwen, known as Robin, a member of Shenzhen’s Doupan Comedy Club (逗伴, pronounced the same as the review site Douban but unrelated to it), the first comedy clubs in the Chinese-speaking world appeared in 2007, when Taiwan's Kamidi club and Hong Kong's Take-Out Comedy were both founded. In 2009 Take-Out Comedy's founder, Jami, helped enthusiasts in Shenzhen start the mainland's first comedy club, Takeout Talk Show. Shanghai and Beijing followed with clubs of their own.

![Students at Beijing Comedy Center (courtesy of Beijing Comedy Center)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702170104eDb2xhIioQ4ElCsZ.jpg-w600)

These clubs generally hold open-mic practice in bars, and in the early years performances went no further than bars and small theaters. In 2011 Takeout Talk Show was the first to move stand-up into a large theater, and the Shanghai and Beijing clubs began playing big rooms more and more often.

Under the influence of those first-tier cities, from 2014 on, Guangzhou, Xiamen, Zhengzhou, Xi'an, Nanning and other cities started clubs too. But the events and shows these "second-tier" clubs put on stay small and irregular.

Shi Laoban thinks stand-up in China can so far be called a cultural phenomenon at most; "as an industry it's zero." "There's basically no market to speak of, no professional workforce, no base of regular audiences. The trade has no established environment and no market order, and it's very hard to make a living at it full time. It hasn't existed long enough — individuals may succeed, but there are too few of them to judge by."

Next to Britain and the United States, with their complete chain of business and clear ladders to climb, stand-up in China is barely started — but it is growing fast.

Feng Liwen dates the change to 2012, when Dragon TV launched *Tonight 80's Talk Show*, the first Chinese program to solicit jokes from comedy fans. The rise of online video, televised comedy talent shows and internet radio — *Diors Man*, Kaola FM and others — also began buying material from joke writers in bulk, letting some comedians turn professional as writers, which at least counted as working in stand-up.

The real turn came in the summer of 2015, when Shanghai's Xiaoguo Culture Media, long a supplier of material to *Tonight 80's Talk Show*, signed several comedians who had been the show's lead writers, plus more than a dozen grassroots performers in Shanghai, Shenzhen, Beijing and Guangzhou. They became China's first crop of professional stand-up comedians, performing weekly in Shanghai, Beijing and elsewhere, and they sped the form's growth enormously.

Last year, according to *The New York Times*, Sohu announced a partnership with the famous American comedy show *Saturday Night Live* to make a Chinese version, and it too went on to sign a group of comedians.

Xijiangyue is fairly optimistic about the trade's prospects: China has a tradition of consuming comedy, he says, and there is room in the market.

Dashan agrees. "China absorbs outside culture very well. The big trend here now is a shift from one monolithic culture to a highly varied one. Niche cultures are popular, you don't have to suit every taste, and you shouldn't expect to. China now looks a lot like America in the '60s. During the Second World War Americans watched the same movies and sang the same songs; after the war the economy took off, the war faded, young people took to alternative culture, and stand-up came out of it."

But more than one comedian voiced the same quiet fear: if the government ever decides to clean up and clamp down on stand-up, this fragile trade dies at once.

Let's hope that stays a bad joke.
